commotion

/kuh-MOH-shun/ · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Commotion means a burst of confused and noisy disturbance breaking out in one place.

When a parrot escaped its cage inside the grocery store, the squawking, the tipped-over displays, and the shrieking shoppers created a commotion in every aisle.

Example

Halfway through the spelling quiz, a wasp drifted in through the open window, and within seconds the silent classroom erupted in commotion: chairs scraped, students ducked and yelled, and papers went flying.

The room goes from total silence to noisy, confused disorder in seconds, with shouting and scrambling everywhere at once. That sudden burst of disorganized noise and movement is exactly what a commotion is.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

uproar: An uproar is a storm of protest or excitement from many people reacting to something, and it can build and last for days across a whole community. A commotion is a burst of on-the-spot noise and confused movement in one place, over almost as soon as it begins.

ruckus: A ruckus is a noisy disturbance with a rowdy, quarrelsome edge: raised voices, maybe a scuffle, usually someone causing trouble. A commotion is broader and more innocent, any sudden flurry of noise and confusion, whether the cause is a quarrel or a loose squirrel.

hubbub: A hubbub is the thick, busy noise of many voices filling a crowded place, like a cafeteria at noon. It is continuous background sound, not an event. A commotion is an event: it breaks out, turns every head, and dies down again.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

calm: a state of peace, quiet, and order

stillness: complete quiet with no movement at all

Where it sits · how big and wild the disturbance grows

stir → commotion → pandemonium

stir vs. commotion: A stir is a small ripple of interest or noise, but a commotion fills the whole room with confused shouting and movement.

pandemonium vs. commotion: A commotion is loud and disorderly, but pandemonium is total, out-of-control chaos with no order left at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — com-: together, thoroughly

Root — mot: to move (Latin movere, motus)

Suffix — -ion: act or state of

Put it together: Com- ('together, thoroughly') plus mot ('to move') plus -ion ('state of') literally builds 'a state of everything being moved at once,' which is exactly what a scene of noisy, confused disturbance feels like.

Use the root in a new word: motivate: A good coach knows how to motivate tired players to keep moving in the final quarter.

Root Check

Word Choice

Neutral / everyday

Common in everyday speech and news writing, usually in phrases like 'cause a commotion' or 'a commotion broke out.' A commotion is about noise and confusion, not danger or failure: a scene can be a commotion without anyone getting hurt. Do not confuse it with 'motion,' which is simply movement.
